parsed.paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 006 - What Critical Scholars Say About Jesus' Bodily Resurrection - Gary Habermas

stories.title_or_label: John Cook's thesis statement on Paul's bodily resurrection
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas recounts John Cook's two-volume work on crucifixion and resurrection published in the German Wissenschaftliche series, and Cook's upfront thesis statement.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Cook begins his volume by stating his thesis: Paul's view of resurrection is that he saw the same body described in the Gospels, not a 'Casper the friendly ghost' view. Habermas notes this was extremely unpopular when published but is now widely accepted.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Surprise and admiration at a credentialed scholar taking an unpopular position that later gained acceptance.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That a credentialed scholar (Cook) publicly argued Paul taught bodily resurrection, and that this view gained acceptance.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Paul actually taught bodily resurrection, or that Cook's thesis is correct; only that Cook asserted it and it became widely taught.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Cook did not make this claim, or that his thesis was not widely adopted.

stories.notes: Anecdote about scholarly reception, not evidence for the resurrection itself.

stories.title_or_label: Dale Allison's personal testimony about the disciples seeing Jesus
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas reads a single sentence from Dale Allison's third volume on resurrection, noting Allison's scholarly credentials (doctoral dissertation at Duke) and personal acquaintance.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Allison writes: 'I believe that the disciples saw Jesus and that he saw them and next Easter will find me in church.' Habermas finds this stunning given Allison's generally non-bodily-leaning views.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: High; Habermas calls it 'the winner' and 'pretty cool,' emphasizing its rhetorical force.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Dale Allison personally affirms the disciples saw Jesus and that he will be in church at Easter.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the resurrection occurred, or that Allison affirms bodily resurrection; Allison explicitly says he is 'more open to non-bodily things.'
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Allison did not write this sentence or does not hold this personal view.

stories.notes: Personal testimony; its emotional power does not transfer warrant to the claim that Jesus rose bodily.

stories.setting_or_context: Habermas recalls Tom Wright's comparison of the resurrection's historical solidity to Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Wright reportedly said the resurrection is as solid to him as Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon. Habermas and the interviewer confirm the quote and its source.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Moderate; Habermas says it didn't stun him because he doesn't buy it, but finds it startling.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Tom Wright made an analogy comparing the resurrection's historical knowability to the Rubicon crossing.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the resurrection is actually as historically solid as the Rubicon crossing; the analogy asserts rather than demonstrates equivalence.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Wright did not make this comparison.

stories.notes: Analogy is a rhetorical device, not evidence; the comparison itself is the claim, not proof of it.

stories.setting_or_context: Habermas mentions Gundry's book 'Soma' (Greek for body) as one of the first treatments on the subject, aimed primarily at refuting Bultmann's view of the body.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Gundry wrote 'Soma' specifically to take on Bultmann's influential non-physical view of resurrection, arguing for a bodily understanding.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Low; presented as a scholarly fact.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Gundry wrote a book called 'Soma' arguing against Bultmann's view of the body.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Gundry's argument is correct, or that Bultmann's view is wrong.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Gundry did not write 'Soma' or did not target Bultmann.

stories.notes: Bibliographic anecdote; the existence of a book does not establish its thesis.

stories.title_or_label: Bultmann's distinction between Paul's belief and his own
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas clarifies that Bultmann can acknowledge Paul believed in bodily resurrection while personally rejecting it, and that Allison makes a similar distinction.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas warns against conflating what Paul said with what Bultmann believed: Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but 'I don't.' Allison similarly distinguishes his own view from Paul's.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Bultmann distinguished Paul's belief in bodily resurrection from his own rejection of it.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Paul actually believed in bodily resurrection, or that Bultmann's rejection is warranted.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Bultmann did not make this distinction.

stories.notes: Conceptual clarification rather than a narrative; included as an illustrative distinction.

narrative_arc.opening_device: Habermas is asked for a memorable quote from volume three, and he says there will be 'a lot of those.'
narrative_arc.central_tension: Critical scholars, including skeptics, increasingly affirm that Paul and the early Christians believed in bodily resurrection, contrary to earlier scholarly consensus.
narrative_arc.resolution_or_payoff: Habermas presents a series of startling quotes from Cook, Allison, Wright, and Gundry, culminating in Allison's personal testimony as 'the winner.'

parsed.notes: The chapter is largely a curated list of scholarly quotations and anecdotes rather than a sustained narrative. Stories function rhetorically to show that even skeptical scholars concede the early Christian belief in bodily resurrection; none of the stories independently establish the resurrection itself.
